title: Completion turns reflection symmetry into a real-rootedness problem
claim: Riemann's theta-integral construction, the later separation of gamma and pole artifacts, and the affine substitution s=1/2+it form one normalization chain: completion makes the reflection s↦1−s exact, while centering at its fixed line converts RH into reality of the zeros of an even entire function of t.
historical_or_program_relation: The original split-reflect-center integral makes symmetry visible; the later completed-xi formulation isolates precisely which zeta zeros remain and packages that symmetry as the modern real-rootedness formulation.
limits: Completion and evenness constrain zero geometry but do not establish that zeros exist on, or all lie on, the critical line; the confinement argument also depends on prior Euler-product nonvanishing and the functional equation.

title: Logarithms, transforms, residues, and Möbius inversion form the prime-zero round trip
claim: Taking the logarithm of the Euler product makes multiplicative prime-power data additive; Mellin/Perron inversion and contour residues then express its weighted summatory function through analytic singularities, especially nontrivial zeros; Möbius inversion is the separate final operation that removes prime-power repetitions to recover primes alone.
historical_or_program_relation: Riemann's prime-power explicit formula becomes a reusable analytic-number-theory pipeline in the later expositions: encode coefficients by a Dirichlet series, continue and shift, read residues, and only then invert the iterate structure when the target is primes rather than prime powers.
limits: The transformations require their own convergence, continuation, contour, truncation, and error estimates; a zero-sum formula neither proves RH nor licenses arbitrary rearrangement of conditionally convergent zero terms.

title: Perron inversion trades sharp cutoffs against decay and finite-frequency resolution
claim: The Perron kernel is not by itself a justified coefficient-sum inverse: in the full contour proof, subtracting the pre-cutoff terms and shifting by the first surviving exponent creates the horizontal-edge decay, whereas truncating the vertical integral replaces exact inversion by a quantified loss concentrated near the cutoff discontinuity.
historical_or_program_relation: The exact generalized-Dirichlet-series argument identifies representation design as the decay mechanism; the modern truncated form exposes contour height T as a resolution budget and makes that same transform usable in explicit estimates.
limits: The exact and truncated formulas have different hypotheses and conclusions, the half-weight at a jump is part of the inversion convention, and neither form supplies analytic continuation or zero-free information on its own.

title: Local zero witnesses become complete only when matched to a global count
claim: Critical-line sign changes and Rolle-interlaced derivative zeros provide local witnesses, while the argument principle supplies an exhaustive multiplicity count; equality of the two closes the classification. In large computations, rigorous sign-error margins, endpoint closure, count identities, and targeted reruns are the additional interfaces that make this abstract witness-plus-count architecture a finite certificate.
historical_or_program_relation: The same proof pattern appears in analytic classification of derivative zeros and in finite RH verification, with computation adding explicit control of floating-point signs and bookkeeping vulnerabilities to the classical argument-principle closure.
limits: The derivative-zero classification is a different region and object from critical-line zeta verification; the computational conclusion is finite-height only, and overlap across related implementations is not the same as independently developed verification.

title: A verified zero range and an asymptotic zero-free region can be spliced into an all-range prime bound
claim: A certified zero count through height H covers the low spectral range, an explicit zero-free inequality covers heights above H, and choosing its parameter at the crossover turns the two inputs into one hypothesis for a shifted-contour explicit-formula bound; published finite-range estimates and a terminal computation then patch the remaining small-x intervals.
historical_or_program_relation: Large-scale zero verification was reused not as evidence for global RH but as one bounded component of an explicit prime-number-theorem estimate, with contour optimization and range patching carrying the information from zeros to ψ and related functions.
limits: Finite RH verification does not imply the full hypothesis, the asymptotic region remains essential above H, and the resulting constants inherit the stated verification, numerical-error, monotonicity, and explicit-formula assumptions.

title: Smoothing replaces a conditionally ordered zero sum by a stable prime-zero factorization
claim: In an unsmoothed explicit formula, vertical contour truncation induces a canonical magnitude ordering of zero terms and that ordering is part of the formula. Mellin smoothing instead makes the logarithmic-derivative identity absolutely convergent enough to integrate and exponentiate into prime and zero factors; changing the cutoff moves contribution between those factors while their product is designed to remain stable.
historical_or_program_relation: The conditional-summation warning already present in Riemann's expansion becomes a design criterion for later numerical reconstruction and motivates the smoothed hybrid Euler-Hadamard representation.
limits: Smoothing changes the represented observable and does not justify rearranging the original series; the reported cutoff compensation is a numerical representation check, not by itself a proof of the hybrid theorem or of RH.

title: Prime powers switch from native signal to removable or structural terms according to the representation
claim: The logarithmic derivative and explicit formula naturally produce weighted prime powers, so retaining them avoids an unnecessary Möbius inversion during zero-based reconstruction. For log-value statistics, however, the averaging family decides their role: higher powers and squares are negligible errors in the height family, while prime squares survive quadratic-character averaging and create the symplectic mean shift.
historical_or_program_relation: Riemann's separation of primes from repetitions develops into a representation-selection rule: keep prime powers when they diagonalize the prime-zero transform, but decompose them by exponent when family averaging can promote one layer into a leading statistic.
limits: The height and quadratic-character families have different averaging symmetries, so negligibility in one cannot be transferred to the other; retaining prime powers reconstructs a weighted density, not the ordinary prime indicator.

title: A spectral zero model is judged by whether zeros emerge from its domain rather than being encoded into it
claim: Connes's quotient construction makes zeros arise as the distributional support left when multiplication by an L-factor fails to force density, whereas the difference-operator proposal obtains Hurwitz-zeta formal eigenfunctions and imposes boundary evaluation to select zeta zeros. Comparing them isolates the decisive Hilbert–Pólya obligation: construct a natural domain, adjoint, and completeness theory that produces the zero condition without defining the space from the desired spectrum.
historical_or_program_relation: Both programs move beyond a bare list of eigenvalues to an operator-space mechanism, but the answer-encoding diagnostic in the trace-formula program sharply exposes the unresolved inverse choice and boundary-domain work in the formal Hamiltonian proposal.
limits: The Connes support classification is not a self-adjoint operator with the zeros as ordinary eigenvalues, while the difference-operator similarity is formal and noninvertible on periodic functions; neither unit establishes spectral reality or RH.

title: Spectral pairing symmetries do not supply the sign or self-adjointness needed for RH
claim: The completed functional equation and modified PT symmetry both organize zeros or proposed eigenvalues into reflected/conjugate pairs, but neither pairing forces fixed-line location or real spectrum. The missing strengthening must be something like a legitimate self-adjoint domain or a geometrically forced sign condition, not another restatement of symmetry.
historical_or_program_relation: Classical completion identifies the symmetry that RH would sharpen; random-matrix and finite-field analogies suggest self-adjointness or negativity, while the PT construction demonstrates concretely why a weaker pairing symmetry can remain compatible with off-line zeros.
limits: PT is analyzed only for proposed formal states, the finite-field and random-matrix comparisons do not transfer a classical operator or intersection form, and naming self-adjointness or negativity does not construct either mechanism.

title: Theta-derived moments feed two different finite encodings of xi zero geometry
claim: Fourier inversion expresses a theta kernel through Xi so that even derivatives become moments used to amplify an eventual sign, while a theta-tail Laplace representation makes the central Taylor coefficients positive moments whose finite windows form Jensen polynomials. Saddle-controlled coefficient ratios then prove an eventual Hermite hyperbolicity regime, whereas the exact all-degree, all-shift hyperbolicity family is equivalent to RH.
historical_or_program_relation: The older moment-sign route uses theta structure to force infinitely many critical-line zeros; the Jensen program repackages related central derivative data into algebraically testable finite polynomials and separates universal Hermite behavior from the unresolved global criterion.
limits: The frozen older unit stops before its final contradiction, eventual Jensen hyperbolicity is much weaker than hyperbolicity for every required degree and shift, and neither an asymptotic Hermite limit nor infinitely many line zeros proves RH.

title: Random matrices model local zero correlations while prime structure supplies missing arithmetic factors
claim: Unfolded zeta zeros and characteristic-polynomial spectra share local statistical behavior after the mean density is removed, but moment constants and mesoscopic covariance retain Euler-product information: the arithmetic factor must be added separately, and near one the logarithmic zeta pole generated by coherent primes sets the covariance scale.
historical_or_program_relation: Random-matrix evidence shifts from a Hilbert–Pólya clue to one component of hybrid models; the mismatch in moment constants and the prime derivation of covariance identify exactly which information the spectral universal model forgets.
limits: Statistical agreement does not construct the missing classical cohomology or self-adjoint operator, the arithmetic factorization is model-dependent, and the cited covariance result is finite-dimensional and does not establish a pathwise field or RH.

title: Smoothing determines whether a few zeros certify oscillation or many zeros resolve prime peaks
claim: For a smoothed summatory error, tail bounds and finite-dimensional phase alignment can let one low zero pair force oscillation. By contrast, reconstructing localized prime-power peaks from a Gaussian-smoothed explicit formula requires a broad, correctly ordered frequency band: ordinates determine peak locations, real parts determine amplitudes, and the zero cutoff fixes the reliable spatial range.
historical_or_program_relation: The two uses of zeros expose complementary transform regimes—low-frequency certification of a global oscillation and high-bandwidth synthesis of local arithmetic detail—so the number of zeros required is controlled by smoothing and target resolution rather than by one universal cutoff rule.
limits: The observables, kernels, and error goals differ; empirical reconstruction endpoints do not bound the full omitted tail, while phase-alignment oscillation does not recover individual primes or locate the first sign reversal.

title: Exact finite certification and asymptotic inference answer different questions
claim: A computation can certify every zero in a bounded rectangle while remaining silent about a limiting Gram-block law or global RH; independently, iterated-logarithm growth shows how a rigorously unbounded zero-driven term can remain visually flat long enough for an opposing finite-range prime-count bias to dominate all feasible data.
historical_or_program_relation: The growth of verified-height computations strengthens bounded certificates, while later oscillation theory explains why extending those bounds cannot by itself settle asymptotic sign or probabilistic behavior.
limits: Slow eventual oscillation does not undermine a correct finite certificate, the cited decomposition of the bias is heuristic in form, no first reversal is located, and the observed Gram distributions are not proved to converge.

title: Short-sum cancellation reaches primes only through a sequence of representation interfaces
claim: Taylor polynomialization, Hölder duplication, Vinogradov mean values, and rational approximation first produce cancellation in short sums of n^(−it); blockwise Abel summation transfers that saving to zeta near one; Euler-product positivity and local zero terms then convert the zeta bound into zero exclusion; finally a shifted Perron contour turns the zero-free region into a prime-number-theorem error term.
historical_or_program_relation: This analytic program records a causal chain from oscillatory-sum technology to prime distribution, with each stage changing representation and exposing a new proof obligation rather than treating an improved PNT error as a direct consequence of a single estimate.
limits: Every transfer is range- and parameter-dependent, the local zero-repulsion and final contour estimates require their stated growth bounds, and the resulting unconditional error remains far from the square-root scale that RH would imply.
